# Frustrations of a microservices developer
At my current job we use a microservices architecture, to run our full system
it requires 15+ services to be running. The seperation of services is great for
scalability and maintainability, but it can be a pain to work with. The
[_Majestic Monolith_](https://signalvnoise.com/svn3/the-majestic-monolith/)
proponents has a point in that you impose a fairly large amount of complexity on
your developers when you go full microservices.

## The need for a full system
When developing a new feature you typically don't need to run all services, you
can test the feature in isolation with unit and acceptance tests. The problem
arises when you need to do a full end-to-end test of the feature or when you need
to debug an issue that spans multiple services. Other benefits of being able to
run a full system locally is that you can demo features in full and get feedback
from stakeholders.

## Requirements to run multiple services
I've tried running multiple microservices before, both via a simple script that
ran a bunch of `dotnet run, npm start, python app.py` and similar commands.
While this works, it's not ideal. The script is platform dependent and you need
to start dependent services such as database etc manually.
This can be simplified via docker-compose, but it's still not ideal. When I last
tried docker-compose it was slow and had some issues with networking. I hear
the file sync has gotten better but I havn't used it extensively since then.
